column6: 'Does one thing' — the test is not task count but WHO requests changes: count distinct actors, not functions.

column3: A 3000-line deity on a cloud named Manager.java: weather, payroll, and toaster settings all require kneeling before it — touch its robe and lightning (merge conflicts) strikes the whole team.
column4: Anti-pattern: one class that knows or does nearly everything, hoarding state and logic that every other part must go through.
column5: class AppManager: # 6k lines / users; orders; ui; cache; email / def do_everything(...)
column6: Facade — a facade is a thin door over subsystems that keep the logic; a god object contains all the logic itself.

column3: A bento box: rice, fish, and pickles in walled compartments — the wasabi never bleeds into the pudding. One flavor per cell.
column4: Split a system so each part addresses one concern (UI, logic, storage), letting each evolve and be understood alone.
column5: routes.py # HTTP concern / service.py # business rules / repo.py # persistence
column6: SRP — SoC partitions the whole architecture by topic; SRP applies actor-based pressure to each class.

column3: A pinball machine with a sealed glass top but an OPEN expansion slot on the side: snap in new bumpers without ever unscrewing the glass over the working table.
column4: Software should be open for extension but closed for modification: add behavior via new code, not edits to tested code.
column5: new PaymentMethod subclass ships / new behavior; process() is untouched
column6: Immutability — immutability freezes runtime data; OCP freezes existing SOURCE while welcoming new modules.

column3: A power strip screwed onto the engine block: mechanics plug new gadgets into labeled sockets; nobody ever splices wires into the loom itself.
column4: Deliberate seams—hooks, plugin registries, abstract slots—where new behavior can be added without touching core code.
column5: @app.register_plugin('pdf') / class PdfExporter(Exporter): ...
column6: Fork-and-edit — extension points invite additions from outside; forking modifies the core and forfeits upgrades.

column3: A chess coach's binder of laminated STRATEGY cards: slide 'Sicilian' out, slide 'King's Gambit' in — the player (context) plays whatever card sits in the sleeve, never rewired.
column4: Encapsulate interchangeable algorithms behind one interface and inject the choice, so new variants extend without editing callers.
column5: class Shipping(Protocol): / def cost(self, order): ... / order.total(FlatRate()) # or ByWeight()
column6: Template method — template fixes the skeleton in a base class (inheritance); strategy swaps whole algorithms by composition.

column3: One steering wheel wired to two cars welded side by side: Monday you steer the left car's road trip, Tuesday the right's — every turn is a fight. Saw them apart.
column4: Smell: one class keeps changing for different reasons on different occasions—evidence it bundles multiple responsibilities.
column5: UserService edited for auth rules, / then email templates, / then avatar resizing
column6: Shotgun surgery — divergent change: many reasons hit ONE class; shotgun surgery: one reason forces edits across MANY classes.

column3: A house wired with forty light switches labeled FUTURE JACUZZI and MAYBE OBSERVATORY — guests flip them all, nothing happens, but the wiring bill was very real.
column4: Smell: abstractions, hooks, and parameters built for imagined future needs that never arrive, taxing every reader today.
column5: class AbstractUserFactoryProvider: / ... # exactly one subclass, ever
column6: YAGNI — YAGNI is the preventive maxim; speculative generality is the smell you find where it was ignored.

column3: The understudy steps into the lead role mid-show; if even one audience member notices the swap, the understudy has failed LISKOV's audition.
column4: Subtypes must be usable anywhere their base type is expected without breaking the program's expectations.
column5: def drain(b: Battery): b.discharge() / # every Battery subtype must drain safely
column6: Syntactic subtyping — merely compiling is not enough; LSP demands behavioral compatibility with the base contract.

column3: A stretching machine grabs a 'rectangle' by both handles; the square SCREAMS as both its sides move together, crushing the operator's test gauge.
column4: Classic LSP violation: a Square subclassing Rectangle breaks code that sets width and height independently.
column5: r.width = 4; r.height = 5 / assert r.area() == 20 # Square gives 25!
column6: Math intuition — mathematically a square IS a rectangle; behaviorally, with mutable setters, it violates the contract.

column3: The diner's new heir may ACCEPT more coupons than dad did (weaker precondition) and pile portions HIGHER (stronger postcondition) — but never the reverse, or the regulars riot.
column4: Valid subtypes never strengthen preconditions, never weaken postconditions, and preserve base invariants: require less, promise more.
column5: base: needs x >= 0, returns non-null / sub: may accept any x, / must still return non-null
column6: Covariance rules — variance governs the TYPES of params and returns; these rules govern the logical CONTRACT strength.

column3: A vending machine upgrade may dispense a FANCIER snack than promised (narrower return, CO-variant) and accept MORE kinds of coins (wider input, CONTRA-variant) — never stingier or pickier.
column4: Safe override typing: return types may narrow in the subclass (covariant); parameter types may widen (contravariant).
column5: base: def get(self) -> Animal / sub: def get(self) -> Cat # covariant ok / sub may accept wider params too
column6: Generic variance — the same words applied to type parameters of containers (List[Cat] vs List[Animal]), not method overrides.

column3: The heir shoves grandma's BEQUEATHED piano off the moving truck: he signed as heir but refuses the goods. Penguin extends Bird, then throws on fly().
column4: Smell: a subclass inherits methods it does not want and stubs or breaks them—a sign the is-a relationship is wrong.
column5: class Penguin(Bird): / def fly(self): / raise NotImplementedError
column6: Abstract stub — abstract methods are contracts awaiting code; refused bequest actively rejects promises already inherited.

column3: A 40-page diner menu forced on the espresso cart: the barista must stock snails just to sell coffee. Chop the menu into laminated cards, one per stall.
column4: Clients should not be forced to depend on methods they do not use: split fat interfaces into small, client-specific ones.
column5: bad: Machine: print+scan+fax / good: Printer, Scanner protocols; / OldPrinter implements Printer only
column6: SRP — SRP splits by the reasons a CLASS changes; ISP splits by what each CLIENT actually calls.

column3: A costume trunk versus a name badge: the fat interface makes every visitor drag the whole costume trunk on stage; the role interface hands them one badge saying CAN_PAY — all the scene needs.
column4: A fat (header) interface mirrors one class's every method; a role interface captures just the one collaboration a client needs.
column5: fat: IEmployee (32 methods) / role: Payable{pay()}, Promotable{...}
column6: ISP — ISP is the principle; fat versus role interface is the vocabulary naming the disease and its cure.

column3: The penthouse no longer runs cables down into the boiler room; both floors bolt onto a steel INTERFACE beam mid-building, and the boiler crew hangs THEIR pipes up to the beam. The dependency's gravity is inverted.
column4: High-level policy and low-level details both depend on abstractions; abstractions never depend on details.
column5: class Store(Protocol): def save(...): ... / class App: uses Store # points up / class SqlStore(Store): ... # points up
column6: Dependency injection — injection is a delivery technique; inversion is about which direction source dependencies point.

column3: A hospital IV bag drips collaborators straight into the patient's arm — the patient never brews its own medicine. Swap the bag, change the behavior, same patient.
column4: Technique: an object's dependencies are supplied from outside (constructor, setter, parameter) rather than created inside it.
column5: svc = ReportService(db=PostgresDb()) / test = ReportService(db=FakeDb())
column6: Service locator — a locator has the object FETCH deps from a registry; injection PUSHES them in, keeping the object passive.

column3: The HOLLYWOOD casting desk: you leave your headshot (callback) and the studio phones YOU when the scene is ready. Actors who keep calling the studio get blacklisted.
column4: The framework calls your code instead of your code calling the framework: don't call us, we'll call you (Hollywood Principle).
column5: app.on('request', handle) / # the framework invokes handle, not you
column6: DIP — DIP inverts which module owns the abstraction; IoC inverts who holds the flow of control (who calls whom).

column3: A mayfly wearing a wristwatch: born at dawn (constructor), works the day (methods), dissolves at dusk (destructor) — the town clock (runtime) schedules every phase.
column4: The arc from allocation and construction through use to destruction or collection; the object must stay valid at every stage.
column5: obj = Widget() # birth / obj.use() # life / del obj / GC # death
column6: Variable scope — scope ends a NAME; the object may outlive it via other references and die later via GC.

column3: Building a wedding cake: the bottom tier (base) must set before the top tier (derived) goes on; at the party the top tier is eaten first (reverse destruction).
column4: Base-class constructors run before derived ones, and fields initialize in declaration order; destruction runs in reverse.
column5: class B(A): / def __init__(self): / super().__init__() # A's parts first
column6: Virtual call in constructor — reading a not-yet-built field is that pitfall; base-before-derived is the rule beneath it.

column3: Two funerals: the C++ undertaker arrives the second you flatline, paperwork exact; the GC FINALizer is a distracted cousin who might hold a service someday — or skip it entirely.
column4: Code run at object destruction; deterministic destructors (C++) free resources reliably, GC finalizers may run late or never.
column5: def __del__(self): ... # may never run / # prefer 'with' / context managers
column6: Context manager __exit__ — __exit__ runs deterministically at block end; __del__ waits on the collector's whim.

column3: A scuba tank strapped on AS you jump in (constructor) that unclips itself the instant you surface (scope exit) — even if you are dragged out unconscious (exception), the strap still releases.
column4: Resource Acquisition Is Initialization: tie a resource to an object's scope—constructor acquires, destructor releases, even on exceptions.
column5: with open('f') as fh: / data = fh.read() / # closed on every exit path
column6: finally blocks — finally is manual pairing at each call site; RAII bakes release into the type so no caller can forget.

column3: Identical twins hand you two passports: same face and name on the page (equal values), but the fingerprint scanner (memory address) proves two people.
column4: Identity asks: are these the SAME object in memory (is)? Equality asks: do two objects hold equivalent values (==)?
column5: a = [1,2]; b = [1,2] / a == b # True (equal values) / a is b # False (distinct objects)
column6: Java's == — on objects Java's == tests identity; .equals() tests value equality, roughly inverse of Python's habit.

column3: A coat check: the clerk files coats by ticket number (hash), then confirms by face (equals). Twins holding different ticket numbers means one coat is lost in the wrong rack forever.
column4: If two objects are equal they MUST have equal hash codes; violating this silently breaks hash sets and dict lookups.
column5: class P: / def __eq__(s, o): return s.id == o.id / def __hash__(s): return hash(s.id)
column6: The reverse direction — equal hashes do NOT require equal objects (collisions are fine); only equals-implies-same-hash is mandatory.

column3: A ten-euro note versus your dog: swap the note for another tenner and nobody cares (value); swap your dog for an identical-looking one and you very much care (entity).
column4: Value objects are defined only by their attributes (interchangeable, ideally immutable); entities keep a persistent identity over time.
column5: Money(10,'EUR') == Money(10,'EUR') / User(id=7) tracked across renames
column6: DTO — a DTO just ferries data across boundaries; a value object is a domain concept with equality semantics.

column3: Flat-pack furniture delivered in a box stamped NOT A CHAIR YET: until you perform the second assembly ritual, sitting drops you to the floor.
column4: An object is constructed inert and only becomes usable after a separate init/start call - flexible, but it opens the half-initialized-object window constructors exist to prevent.
column5: srv = Server() / srv.configure(cfg) / srv.start()  # safe to use only after both calls
column6: vs constructor/RAII initialization (483): single-phase yields an invariant-complete object at birth; two-phase leaves a gap where methods are unsafe

column3: A master forger who only copies paintings from his OWN studio: he knows which layers are paint and which are glued-on photos, so his duplicates never share canvas with the original.
column4: A constructor that takes an existing instance and builds an independent duplicate - the class itself decides how deep the copy goes.
column5: C++: Point(const Point& p) : x(p.x), y(p.y) {} / Python: Point.from_other(p)
column6: vs clone() methods: same goal, but the constructor states copy depth in the type and avoids Java clone's fragile contract; shallow-vs-deep choice itself lives at 345

column3: A giraffe shipped in a horse-sized crate: the packers SLICE off the neck to make it fit — what arrives is legally a horse. Ship by trailer hitch (pointer or reference) instead.
column4: C++ pitfall: assigning a derived object BY VALUE into a base variable copies only the base part, slicing off subclass data and behavior.
column5: Dog d; Animal a = d; // C++ by value / a.speak(); // Animal's version: tail sliced off
column6: Upcasting via pointer — a Base* or Base& still dispatches to Dog; only by-VALUE copies slice.

column3: Renovating a plane mid-flight without waking the passengers: rip out and rebuild the galley, yet every drink still arrives on time. Behavior identical, structure new.
column4: Restructuring code to improve its design WITHOUT changing observable behavior, in small steps guarded by tests.
column5: tests green -> rename, extract, / inline -> tests still green
column6: Rewrite — a rewrite replaces behavior wholesale with fresh risk; refactoring preserves behavior step by tiny step.

column3: Something reeks under the floorboards of a room where nothing looks wrong: your NOSE (heuristic), not the smoke alarm (compiler), says lift the boards.
column4: A surface symptom in code (odd size, naming, duplication) hinting at a deeper design problem worth investigating—not itself a bug.
column5: 800-line class, 9 params, twin blocks / # compiles fine, still stinks
column6: Bug — a bug produces wrong behavior now; a smell predicts pain later while behavior stays correct.

column3: Two office whiteboards both list the tax rate; an intern updates only one. April arrives soaked in lawsuits — the boards disagreed. Keep ONE board. Keep it DRY.
column4: Don't Repeat Yourself: every piece of knowledge gets a single authoritative representation; duplication forks the truth.
column5: TAX = 0.21 # single source / total = net * (1 + TAX)
column6: Deduplicating lookalike code — DRY is one source of KNOWLEDGE; merging coincidentally similar code couples unrelated things.

column3: One camper packs a KISS-simple folding pocketknife; his buddy hauls a 40-kilo might-need-it trunk (YAGNI violation) up the trail, uses none of it, and wheezes at the summit.
column4: KISS: prefer the simplest design that works. YAGNI: don't build features until actually needed—most 'later' never comes.
column5: need CSV export today? / write csv_export() / not ExportFrameworkFactory
column6: Underengineering — KISS/YAGNI trim speculation, never required correctness: simplest thing that WORKS, not almost works.

column3: Mountain camp: inside each tent the gear is packed tight and orderly (cohesion); between tents runs just one thin rope (coupling). Cross-lace fifty ropes and one slip drags every tent off the cliff.
column4: Aim for low coupling (few, thin dependencies between modules) and high cohesion (each module's parts belong tightly together).
column5: cohesive: Wallet{balance, add, spend} / coupled: Wallet reads UI.textbox
column6: Encapsulation — encapsulation is a mechanism inside one class; coupling and cohesion measure between and within modules.

column3: A single run-on sentence tattooed down someone's whole arm, wrist to shoulder; readers keep rotating the arm and losing their place. Paragraphs exist for a reason.
column4: Smell: a function long enough to need scrolling, with comments as section headers—each labeled chunk wants extracting.
column5: def process(): # 300 lines / # -- validate -- / # -- price -- # comments = seams
column6: Large class — a large class hoards many responsibilities at type level; a long method crams many steps into one function.

column3: A neighbor who cooks every meal in YOUR kitchen: opens your fridge, uses your knives, then carries dinner back home. Move him in (move the method) or change the locks.
column4: Smell: a method that mostly reads and manipulates ANOTHER object's data—move the method to where the data lives.
column5: def total(order): / return order.qty * order.price / # lives outside Order: move it in
column6: Law of Demeter violation — Demeter counts dots in a call chain; feature envy asks which class should OWN the logic.

column3: A wizard mutters '86400' and '0.21' over the cauldron — apprentices copy the MAGIC NUMBERS wrong and the potion explodes. Label the vials: SECONDS_PER_DAY, TAX_RATE.
column4: Smell: raw ints/strings and bare literals stand in for domain concepts; wrap them in named constants and small types.
column5: bad: if status == 3: retry(86400) / good: if status == Status.FAILED: / retry(SECONDS_PER_DAY)
column6: Value object — the value object (Money, Email) is the CURE that replaces obsessive primitives with real types.

column3: A dentist EXTRACTS one tangled tooth from the jaw (long method) and mounts it on its own little stand with a nameplate — the jaw finally closes, and the tooth can be inspected alone.
column4: Refactoring: pull a coherent code fragment into a new well-named method and call it, turning comments into names.
column5: # -- validate input -- becomes: / validate_input(order) / # the name replaces the comment
column6: Inline method — inline is the exact inverse: dissolve a needless method back into its caller.

column3: A scout troop crossing a campsite: each kid pockets ONE piece of litter on the way through; by season's end the forest floor gleams, though no cleanup day was ever held.
column4: Always leave the code a little cleaner than you found it: tiny opportunistic cleanups on every visit compound into health.
column5: while fixing a bug: / rename tmp2 -> retry_count, / delete the dead branch
column6: Big-bang refactor — the scout rule is continuous micro-cleanup in passing; a dedicated rewrite is a separate scheduled effort.
